title: Should You Frame Cross Stitch With Glass or Without Glass?

seo.title: Should You Frame Cross Stitch With Glass or Without Glass?
seo.meta_description: Pros and cons of framing cross stitch with glass, acrylic or no glazing, and why the stitched surface should usually be kept away from the glazing.
seo.search_intent: Stitchers framing a finished piece who are deciding whether to use glass, acrylic or leave the textile open.

excerpt: Glass protects against dust and handling, but it should not press directly on the stitches. An open textile finish can also be appropriate in some situations.
content_html:
There is no rule saying every cross stitch must be framed behind glass, and there is no rule saying glass automatically harms embroidery. The choice depends on where the piece will hang, how much protection you want from dust and handling, whether the design contains beads or dimensional stitches, and how the frame is constructed.

The more important question is not simply “glass or no glass.” It is whether a rigid glazing surface will press directly against the stitching. When glass or acrylic is used, a mat or framing spacers can create separation.

Glass protects against dust, handling and accidental contact

An uncovered textile gradually collects dust. In an ordinary living space it may also encounter small splashes, smoke residue or hands brushing the surface during cleaning.

Glazing creates a physical barrier that reduces this exposure. That can be useful for gifts, high-traffic rooms and projects representing many hours of work.

It does not make the piece immune to environmental damage. Light and humidity still matter, but routine cleaning no longer requires touching the stitched fabric itself.

The stitches should not be pressed directly against the glazing

When crosses touch glass, their texture can be flattened. Any moisture present also has less space to dissipate between textile and glazing.

A mat or purpose-made frame spacer can hold the glass or acrylic away from the stitched surface. Only a small air gap is required.

Beads, French knots and charms need additional clearance so the highest elements are not compressed.

Acrylic is a lighter alternative to glass

Acrylic weighs less and does not break like ordinary glass, which can be useful for large frames or locations where breakage is a concern.

UV-filtering versions are available, just as there are different grades of framing glass. Actual protection depends on the product specifications rather than the material name alone.

Acrylic can scratch more easily during cleaning. Use appropriate cleaning materials and avoid rubbing a dusty surface dry.

No glazing gives a very direct view of textile texture

An open frame lets the relief of the stitches remain visually immediate and avoids reflections. It can work beautifully for small decorative pieces.

The tradeoff is exposure. Removing dust from mounted embroidery is more delicate than wiping the front of a glazed frame.

If you choose no glazing, avoid kitchens, bathrooms, smoke and locations where the piece will be touched regularly. A dry, relatively clean indoor wall is a better environment.

Direct light matters with or without glass

Ordinary glass does not make a sunny window a safe place for embroidery. Prolonged strong light can affect thread and fabric color.

For important pieces, hang the frame away from direct sun and consider glazing with documented UV filtering. No glazing system eliminates every effect of light.

Reflection matters too. On a wall opposite windows, anti-reflective glazing may make the stitching significantly easier to see.

Choose based on the piece and its environment

For a valuable project, long-term gift or room where dust is common, separated glass or acrylic offers practical protection.

For a mini piece, decorative hoop finish or textile where you want maximum visible texture and can easily clean or reframe it, leaving the piece open may be reasonable.

For beads and dimensional elements, check frame depth before deciding. Clearance can matter more than the exact glazing material.

Glass does not inherently damage cross stitch. Problems are more likely when mounting compresses the textile or unsuitable materials are used. If you want glazing, keep it off the stitches and avoid direct sunlight. If you prefer an open finish, accept the additional care required for dust and handling.

Future maintenance matters too. With glazing, routine dust can be removed from the front surface without touching the textile. An open piece may eventually need a very soft brush, careful low-suction cleaning or partial disassembly when dust settles deeply into the fabric.

In humid conditions, never close a frame around stitching that is still damp after washing. Glass does not create moisture by itself, but sealing residual moisture inside a frame can encourage condensation and staining.

Transport is another factor. Acrylic reduces weight and breakage risk on a large frame, while glass generally offers a harder surface against minor scratches. The best choice can depend as much on size and location as on appearance.

For an heirloom or expensive custom frame, ask how the glazing is spaced and what materials touch the textile rather than simply requesting “glass.” The complete framing package matters more than one component considered in isolation.

For small seasonal pieces, removable framing can also make no-glass display more practical because the textile can be cleaned or remounted between uses.
